name: Bù Gia Mập
headline: Basalt roads and highland water.
subheadline: Waterfalls, volcanic textures, and quiet forest air.
introduction: Đắk Nông is a quieter highland route: basalt soil, open roads, waterfalls, forest pockets, and a slower kind of green.
shortDescription: A highland nature stop with waterfalls, volcanic textures, open roads, and quiet Central Highlands air.
description: A forest trail-running trip that turned into new friends, muddy roads, and the start of more outdoor suffering.
longDescription: This is not a place to rush. The appeal is in the road, the pauses between waterfalls, and the feeling of being away from the usual city-to-beach loop.
overview:
I went to Bù Gia Mập to practice trail running in the forest with my boss. That simple plan somehow opened the door to new friends who liked the same kind of suffering, which then led to more trail trips later.

Some hobbies start with gear. Mine started with mud, trees, and trying not to breathe too loudly.
weatherNote: Dry months make road days simpler. Waterfall areas can still be slippery, so keep footwear practical.
travelTips: Keep the route simple and leave time between nature stops.
Bring shoes that can handle wet paths.
Download maps before leaving the main town.
notFor: Travelers who need polished tourism infrastructure.

images.title: Sunbeams Through Bamboo Canopy
images.story: About an hour into the morning run, the canopy opened just enough for a shaft of sun to cut through the rising humidity. Everyone paused to catch their breath and pretend we stopped strictly for the view. The cool early air was already giving way to heavy forest heat.

images.title: Spiderweb Across the Trail
images.story: Running headfirst into a web is usually the hazard of leading the trail pack. Luckily, this one caught the morning backlight at eye level just before I crashed through it. We admired the silk geometry for a second and ducked around the side.

images.title: Wild Fungi on Forest Floor
images.story: Looking down while navigating slippery tree roots reveals a whole quiet world beneath the mud. These two pale mushrooms had popped up along a mossy log on the damp floor. In a rainforest this wet, decay and fresh growth share the exact same patch of ground.

images.title: Rocky Stream in the Woods
images.story: We hit the river crossing right around midday when the heat started pressing down between the trees. Walking across meant stepping across slick basalt rocks and accepting that our trail shoes would stay drenched for the rest of the day. The highland water was numbingly cold and completely revived our legs.

images.title: Mackerel Clouds Above the Canopy
images.story: A rare break in the tall forest trees finally let us see what the sky was doing above us. Puffy mackerel clouds were drifting across an open patch of blue, framed by heavy green branches. After hours trapped under a dense ceiling, it felt good to realize the horizon was still up there.

images.title: Silhouetted Leaves Against the Sky
images.story: I leaned back against a rock during a water break and pointed the camera straight up. The dark canopy formed a jagged lattice against the blue sky, letting only dappled afternoon light filter through. Out here, you measure the day not by a watch, but by how much sky you can actually see.

images.title: Current Over Dark Basalt
images.story: After hours of churning red mud, finding this clear stream felt like hitting an unexpected jackpot. The water poured over slick black basalt into a cold pool, foaming white under patches of high canopy sun. We rinsed our calves and soaked our shoes before talking ourselves into running again.

images.title: Guarded Guinea Pig Break
images.story: At a small rest post near the trail exit, this little tricolor guinea pig sat tucked beneath a wire dome. Someone had woven fresh green stalks through the bars to keep it occupied while we collapsed onto benches nearby. It watched our muddy shoes with total indifference and kept steadily chewing.

images.title: Mist Rolling Over the Greenhouses
images.story: Winding our way out along the ridge road, thick cloud rolled in and smothered the entire valley below. Long white greenhouses clustered along the lower slopes, barely peeking through the gray drift. It felt like the highlands were sealing themselves back up after two days of sweat.
